title: Relative Major and Minor
description: Every major key has a minor twin that uses exactly the same notes. Here's how to find it.

steps.title: Two keys, one set of notes
steps.description: Every major key has a relative minor. It uses the very same notes, just with a different note as home. To find it, go to the 6th note of the major scale. In C major, count C, D, E, F, G, A. A is the 6th, so A minor is C major's relative minor.

steps.title: C major
steps.description: Play C major, the white keys from C up to B. Listen to how it settles when you get back to C.
steps.hint: All white keys from C to B.

steps.title: A natural minor
steps.description: Now play the white keys from A up to G. Not one key has changed, yet it sounds noticeably darker. The only difference is where home is.
steps.hint: All white keys again, this time starting on A.

steps.title: Finding any relative minor
steps.description:
Quickest way: from the major key's name, count down 3 semitones.

• C major → A minor
• G major → E minor
• D major → B minor
• F major → D minor

Relative keys always share a key signature, so they have the same sharps or flats.

steps.title: C major's home chord
steps.description: Play a C major chord. This is the chord that says 'we're in C major'.

steps.title: A minor's home chord
steps.description: Now A minor. It shares two notes with C major, C and E, and you're still on white keys, but the mood is completely different.
steps.hint: A, C, E. All white keys.

steps.title: Find the relative minor
steps.description: What's the relative minor of G major?
